property_summary: The correct paused() returns the actual contract pause state; the mutant always returns true, so when the contract is unpaused after a pause-unpause cycle, paused() still returns true.
For any call to paused() after the contract is unpaused, the reference returns false, but the mutant returns true.
After the contract is initialized, paused() returns false initially (since _paused defaults to false in __Pausable_init_unchained), but the mutant always returns true.
The reference contract's paused() returns false after initialization and unpausing, but the mutant always returns true.
After any sequence of pause/unpause operations, the reference paused() returns the actual pause state, while the mutant always returns true regardless of pause state.

A call to paused() must return true exactly when the contract has been paused via pause(), but the buggy version always returns false, so after calling pause() the return value fails to reflect the paused state.
After external pause() and unpause(), the contract's paused() return value must match the actual paused state, but the buggy version always returns false even after pause().

After any sequence of pause/unpause calls by authorized roles, paused() must return true if and only if the contract is actually paused; the bug always returns false, violating this after pause() is called.
After calling pause() by an authorized LRT manager, paused() must return true, but the bug makes it return false regardless of pause state.
After an authorized LRT manager calls pause(), paused() must return true; the buggy version always returns false, violating this property.

The paused() function must return the opposite of the internal _paused state; calling pause() then paused() must return true in the reference, but the mutant returns false (since it returns !_paused which is false after _paused is set to true).
After the contract is paused, calling paused() must return true, but the mutant returns false because it inverts the internal state.
For any caller, after pausing the contract, c.paused() must return true; the mutant breaks this by returning !_paused (false).
For any admissible caller, after the contract is paused, paused() must return true; the mutant returns false because it inverts the internal state.
After pausing the contract, paused() must return true. The mutant inverts the return value, so paused() returns false when the contract is paused.
Only addresses with the LRT admin role can successfully update the LRT config; the bug allows an address with only the manager role to succeed, violating access control.
An address granted only the MANAGER role can never successfully update the LRTConfig (call returns false), whereas the buggy version allows it to succeed (call returns true).
An address granted only the LRT manager role can never successfully call updateLRTConfig (call reverts), whereas the buggy version allows such an address to succeed (call does not revert).
Only an address granted the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can successfully change lrtConfig via updateLRTConfig, but the bug allows an address with only the MANAGER role to also change it.
Any address granted only the MANAGER role (and not the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) must cause updateLRTConfig to revert; the bug allows such a manager to succeed.
Only an address with the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can change the LRT config; the mutant allows any caller to update it.

Anyone can call updateLRTConfig on the mutant, while the reference requires DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE; thus after an arbitrary sender calls updateLRTConfig with a valid non-zero address, the reference's lrtConfig remains unchanged but the mutant's lrtConfig updates.
Only the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can successfully call updateLRTConfig, but the mutant allows MANAGER role holders to call it as well.

After any successful call to updateLRTConfig, the address stored in state variable lrtConfig equals the provided new address; the buggy modifier allows MANAGER-role callers to execute the function, but that does not affect the lrtConfig assignment rule — instead, the bug allows MANAGER to call updateLRTConfig when originally only admin could, so we assert that updateLRTConfig always updates lrtConfig to the given address exactly for any caller who passes the role check; the mutant fails this because a MANAGER can successfully call updateLRTConfig and change lrtConfig when the reference would have reverted.

Any call to updateLRTConfig that does not revert must be made by an address holding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE; the mutant wrongly allows MANAGER role holders to succeed, violating the invariant that successful calls imply caller has DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE.
A successful call to updateLRTConfig must come from an address with the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00), but the mutant allows MANAGER-role callers to succeed.
Any call to updateLRTConfig that does not revert must be performed by an address holding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE; the mutant allows callers with only the MANAGER role to succeed, violating this rule.

For any caller, if c.updateLRTConfig(newAddr) is called, it must revert if and only if the caller does not have the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. The bug removes this revert, causing the state-changing function to succeed when called by a non-admin.
The reference C always reverts when updateLRTConfig is called by a non-admin (no DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE), while the buggy version succeeds without revert for at least one non-admin caller.
For any caller that does NOT have DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on the lrtConfig, a call to updateLRTConfig must revert. The bug removes the revert, so a non-admin caller can change the config successfully.

For any caller that does NOT have the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on the lrtConfig, updateLRTConfig must revert; the bug removes the revert check, so a non-admin caller succeeds in changing the config, which can be observed by the state variable not being updated when it should revert.

For any caller lacking the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on the lrtConfig contract, updateLRTConfig must revert and leave the lrtConfig state unchanged; the bug removes the revert, allowing a non-admin to update lrtConfig successfully.
After initialization, the maximum node delegator count must be greater than 0; the bug sets it to 0, making it impossible to ever add a node delegator.

After initialization in the reference contract, calling addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with a single valid address should succeed (not revert), but the bug makes it always revert due to maxNodeDelegatorCount being 0.

After initialize, maxNodeDelegatorCount must be greater than 0 so that adding at least one node delegator does not revert with MaximumNodeDelegatorCountReached; the bug sets it to 0 making any addition revert.

After initialization, nodeDelegatorQueue must start empty and maxNodeDelegatorCount equals 10; the bug sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 0, causing addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with any single valid address to revert with MaximumNodeDelegatorCountReached.

After initialization, maxNodeDelegatorCount must be greater than 0 so that it is possible to add at least one node delegator without reverting; the bug sets it to 0, making any addition revert with MaximumNodeDelegatorCountReached.

After initialization, the value of maxNodeDelegatorCount must equal 10; the mutant sets it to 5, so a call to updateMaxNodeDelegatorCount(10) will emit an event only in the reference but not in the mutant.

After initialization, maxNodeDelegatorCount must strictly equal 10; the mutant sets it to 5, so for any valid address the view function maxNodeDelegatorCount() returns a value different from 10 in the mutant.
After initialization, calling addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with a sufficiently large array fails in the mutant but succeeds in the reference because maxNodeDelegatorCount is smaller.
